clue.text: Teacher made knots in his hair

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the knotted letters sit within the word his

parts.note: taken as written

parts.note: taken as written
a tress is a long lock of hair

explanation.surface: A teacher has tied knots in a boy's hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made knots' reads as 'tied knots', but 'knots' is the anagram signal on MADE, giving EADM; 'in' puts that inside HIS after its H, and TRESS follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A headmistress is the woman in charge of a school, its senior teacher.

clue.text: Meaningful picture from reading out Mog's letters

indicators.note: Reading something out means saying it rather than writing it, so what counts is the noise the characters make in the mouth.

parts.note: the name is spelled M, O, G, and each of those three letters has a spoken name of its own

explanation.walkthrough: Say the three letter-names one after another and they run together into a word borrowed from Japanese, where it means picture-character.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaningful picture -> EMOJI: a tiny symbol typed in place of words, so the picture is doing the carrying that a sentence would otherwise do.

clue.text: Tear up unfashionable husband's old cotton belt?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the word for tear runs backwards

parts.note: to tear along is to speed
out means no longer in fashion
H is the abbreviation for husband, as in genealogy tables

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned husband's cotton belt gets ripped apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' sounds like ripping, but it means to rush, SPEED, and 'up' reverses it to DEEPS. The Deep South is the region of the southern United States where cotton plantations once dominated.
explanation.definitionFit: The Deep South was historically the heart of the American Cotton Belt, the region where cotton was the main crop.

clue.text: Faces court released to the public

parts.note: a defendant who faces something is up against it, and the passive phrase that says so needs this two-letter verb to stand it up
to take someone to court is to sue them, so the person in the dock has been sued

explanation.walkthrough: The whole trick is where the space goes: IS SUED, two words about a courtroom, run together into one word with no law in it at all.
explanation.definitionFit: released to the public -> ISSUED: a statement, a stamp or a passport that has been issued has been put out officially for anyone to have.

clue.text: Grip case with empty travelator ahead

indicators.note: ahead means in front, so the emptied word comes before the word for case
empty means with the contents removed, so only the first and last letters of travelator remain

parts.note: outer letters T and R
a case in law is an action, a lawsuit

explanation.surface: Someone grips a suitcase at an airport, with a deserted moving walkway in front of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks like luggage beside the travelator, but it is a lawsuit, ACTION; 'empty' leaves TR, and 'ahead' puts it first.
explanation.definitionFit: Traction is the grip a tyre or shoe has on a surface, the friction that stops it slipping.

clue.text: Message from girl I am excited about

indicators.note: Taking something from a phrase means lifting it out of what is already written there, one consecutive letter after another.
About means turned round, the way a ship comes about, so the run of letters is read the other way along the entry.

parts.note: five letters in a row, starting in the middle of the first word and stopping just inside the last, read backwards

explanation.walkthrough: The girl is never named and 'I am' is not fodder to be shuffled. Every letter is already sitting in the clue, running the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: Message -> EMAIL: an email is a message sent electronically, so the definition is the general word standing in for one particular kind.

clue.text: Severe wife burning trousers

indicators.note: To trouser something is to pocket it, slipping it out of sight inside, so the letter beside this word goes within the other.

parts.note: singeing is burning at the edges, and the word opens up after its first letter
W is the usual abbreviation for wife

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' is a verb, British slang for quietly pocketing something, and that is the only word telling you one letter goes inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe -> SWINGEING: swingeing cuts or fines are punishingly harsh ones, a British adjective with no connection at all to swinging.

clue.text: Play guitar supporting Prince, an old 21

indicators.note: A support sits under what it holds up, and in a down entry underneath means later, so the guitar work goes below the royal name.

parts.note: the younger of the two British princes born to Charles and Diana
to strum is to play a guitar by sweeping a hand across the strings
the article goes in as the two letters it is spelled with

explanation.walkthrough: A bare number sends you to that clue for the definition, so solve 21 across first. The middle initial stands for nothing: his parents could not choose between two grandfathers.
explanation.definitionFit: old 21 -> HARRY S TRUMAN: 21 across is the acronym for the American president, and Truman held that office from 1945, so he is a past one.

clue.text: Practising lawyers troubling to Morse

indicators.note: Something troubling will not let things settle, and letters that cannot settle finish up in an order nobody gave them.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, exactly the length the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: Morse is the Oxford detective of the television series, and the surface wants you reading him as a code. He is seven letters and a preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: Practising lawyers -> MOOTERS: a moot is the mock case law students argue for training, so mooters practise in the rehearsing sense, not the professional one.

clue.text: 8's scheme for regenerating height with everyone in chocolate factory shrunk?

indicators.note: One thing put in another sits between its parts, so the two short pieces named before this word are buried between the two named after.

parts.note: a Mars is a chocolate bar sold in every British newsagent
a factory is a plant, and it comes up one letter short of that
H is the standard abbreviation for height
all means everyone, every last one of them

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is selling Roald Dahl. The wordplay wants a confectionery brand and an industrial plant instead, and only the brand survives whole.
explanation.definitionFit: 8's scheme for regenerating -> MARSHALL PLAN: the American programme, named for Truman's secretary of state, that funded the rebuilding of western Europe after 1945.

clue.text: Bad mushroom trip's beginning in a frenzy

indicators.note: in means inside, so the opening letter of trip goes within a frenzy

indicators.note: beginning means the first part, so only the opening letter of trip's is used

parts.note: first letter of trip's

explanation.surface: A bad trip on magic mushrooms starts with the user in a wild state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trip' suggests a hallucinogen, which suits the mushroom, but it only gives T; 'in' puts it inside A MANIA, before the last A.
explanation.definitionFit: Amanita is a genus of fungi that includes the death cap and fly agaric, both poisonous toadstools.

clue.text: Vet again checks animal that's caught cold

parts.note: reins are what check a horse, and to rein in is to check

indicators.note: Whatever is caught is held fast inside the thing that caught it, so the letter named after this word sits within the animal.

parts.note: a pet is the animal kept at home, and its three letters open up after two
C is the letter on the cold tap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vet' is the verb — to examine something closely before approving it — and not the animal doctor the pet in the wordplay keeps hinting at.
explanation.definitionFit: Vet again -> REINSPECT: to vet is to examine critically before giving approval, and the re- prefix asks for that examination a second time.

clue.text: Cheap fizz from Majestic brought round

parts.note: regal means majestic, befitting a monarch

explanation.surface: Someone brings a bottle of cheap sparkling wine round from Majestic.
explanation.walkthrough: Majestic Wine is a British wine retailer, so 'Cheap fizz from Majestic' reads as a bargain bottle of bubbly; 'brought round' reverses REGAL instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is a fizzy, inexpensive beer, so it fits as a jokey cheap fizz in place of champagne.

clue.text: Hampshire's opener exploited fault as much as bowler could bear?

definitions.text: as much as bowler could bear?

indicators.note: an opener is what comes first, so only the first letter of Hampshire's is taken

parts.note: first letter of Hampshire's

indicators.note: exploited means worked or manipulated, so the letters of fault are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Hampshire opening batsman took advantage of a fielding error, more than the bowler could stand.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes the bowler a player and the opener a batsman, but a bowler is a hat. 'exploited' rearranges FAULT to ATFUL after H. Hampshire is an English county cricket team.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatful is the amount a hat can hold, and a bowler is a hard round felt hat.

clue.text: B&B owner might stand round here

definitions.text: B&B owner might stand round here

parts.words: B&B owner might stand round here
parts.note: The surface has a landlord standing a round of drinks for his guests, which is the wrong sort of bar altogether.; A round is one slice off a loaf, and 'stand' is literal: at a bed-and-breakfast table the browned slices are stood upright in a wire frame.

explanation.walkthrough: There is no separable wordplay to hunt for — the sentence simply means the object twice over. British breakfast tables stand the slices up so they cool and stay crisp.
explanation.definitionFit: B&B owner might stand round here -> TOAST RACK: a round is a slice of bread, and the wire frame on a breakfast table is where the slices stand.

clue.text: Offer suit to sell back, keeping current winter clothing

back means in reverse, so the word sell is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
I is the symbol for electric current in physics

explanation.definitionFit: Woollies is an informal British word for knitted woollen garments such as jumpers worn in cold weather.

clue.text: Title holder's fallen during road race at the start

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road, and its four letters split after the third

parts.note: race supplies its opening letter alone
someone fallen is down, and the word goes in whole

clue.text: Platonic relationship troubled Macron, in bed mostly

explanation.definitionFit: A bromance is a close but non-sexual friendship between two men, a blend of brother and romance.

clue.text: Biking kit verges on lingerie where she lives

definitions.note: Kit is a mass noun for gear in general while the answer is plural, which is how motorcyclists talk: the jacket and the trousers are named together.

if something is at hers, it is where she lives, and the two words run together

explanation.definitionFit: Biking kit -> LEATHERS: leathers are the thick hide jacket and trousers a motorcyclist wears as armour against the road.

clue.text: Ass kept hidden in apprehension, age-related

clue.text: Date with Mr Bean from the telly outside saloon in US

clue.text: Call up the day before collecting permit

clue.text: Sun now implying this rain?

explanation.definitionFit: School -> KINDERGARTEN: a kindergarten is the class small children attend before formal lessons begin, so it is a school by name and by function.
